## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

{{< include ../learning_objectives/0230-git-merge-conflicts.qmd >}}

One of the major blockers in getting used to version control is dealing with merge conflicts! 😱

Git can automatically handle merging two versions of a file
if each collaborator changes different lines.
However, when two collaborators change the same line, Git throws up its hands
and says, "I cannot handle this responsibility, I need help from a human!"

<img src="https://media.giphy.com/media/4SZxcPTtlGAZa/giphy.gif">

When this happens, your human task is to find the merge conflict markers,
remove them, and settle on which version of the line(s) where the conflict occurred should remain.
Merge conflict markers include:

- `<<<<<<< HEAD` to indicate the beginning of the merge conflict
- `>>>>>>>` to indicate the end of the merge conflict
- `=======` between the markings mentioned above to indicate the boundary between the two proposed changes.
  The version of the change before the separator is your change,
  and the version that follows the separator is the change that existed on GitHub.


:::{.exercise}

We are now going to generate and resolve merge conflicts.
I have set up a template GitHub repository
for you so that you can easily generate a merge conflict to resolve.
We will do this twice, once with a simple plain-text file (*e.g.*, an R script)
and once with a more complex text file (*e.g.*, a Jupyter notebook).

**Resolving merge conflicts in a simple text file:**

1. Copy the `start/` folder of the [`r-cube` demo](https://github.com/UBC-DSCI/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/tree/main/demos/r-cube) to your computer,
   make it a git repository, and push it to a new repository of your own on GitHub
   (see [how to use the demos](https://github.com/UBC-DSCI/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/tree/main/demos)).

2. Open your copy as its own project (in RStudio, Positron or VS Code).

3. Click on the Actions tab,
   and then click on the workflow .github/workflows/main.yml.
   You then should see a “Run workflow” button with a drop-down menu.
   From that menu, select “Run workflow”
   (this will trigger GitHub Actions to create a commit in your remote repository).

4. Locally on your computer, fix the second line in `cube.r` so that it calculates the cube,
   not the square (e.g., change `x^2` to `x^3`).
   Commit your changes to version control via Git and push your changes to GitHub.

5. Resolve the merge conflict so that you can see your changes on GitHub.


**Resolving merge conflicts in a more complex text file:**

1. Copy the `start/` folder of the [`r-cube-notebook` demo](https://github.com/UBC-DSCI/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/tree/main/demos/r-cube-notebook) to your computer,
   make it a git repository, and push it to a new repository of your own on GitHub
   (see [how to use the demos](https://github.com/UBC-DSCI/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/tree/main/demos)).

2. Open your copy as its own project (in RStudio, Positron or VS Code).

3. Click on the Actions tab,
   and then click on the workflow .github/workflows/main.yml.
   You then should see a “Run workflow” button with a drop-down menu.
   From that menu, select “Run workflow”
   (this will trigger GitHub Actions to create a commit in your remote repository).

4. Fix the second line in the code cell in `cube.ipynb` so that it calculates the cube,
   not the square (e.g., change `x^2` to `x^3`).
   Commit your changes to version control via Git and push your changes to GitHub.

5. Resolve the merge conflict so that you can see your changes on GitHub.
:::
